desc:
Every node of a binary tree holds a single bit, 0 or 1. Each root-to-leaf path therefore spells a binary number: read the bits from the root down to the leaf, with the root as the most significant bit. For example the path 1 → 0 → 1 is the number 101 in binary, which is 5.

Return the sum of the numbers spelled by all root-to-leaf paths (a leaf is a node with no children), taken modulo 1,000,000,007. The empty tree has no paths and gives 0.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1] the four paths spell 100, 101, 110 and 111, that is 4 + 5 + 6 + 7, so the answer is 22.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Think about how the number for the path to a node relates to the number for the path to its parent.
Appending a bit b to a binary number x gives 2 * x + b.
Carry the number downward with child = 2 * parent + bit, keeping it modulo 1,000,000,007 because a path can have 1,500 bits. Add the value of every leaf to the answer.
editorial: Let num[v] be the binary number spelled by the path from the root to node v. Appending one more bit shifts the number left by one position and adds the bit, so num[child] = 2 * num[parent] + bit(child) and num[root] = bit(root). The answer is the sum of num over all leaves.

A path may be 1,500 nodes long, which is far beyond 64 bits, so every update is done modulo 1,000,000,007. This is safe because the recurrence only uses additions and multiplications. In the level-order array parents come before children, so one forward pass over the real nodes is enough.
O(n) time, O(n) space for the numbers (the values can also be passed down a stack/recursion instead).
